Figure 24: Commercially available (a) header and (b) serpentine MCHXs [20] On the other hand, commercially-available serpentine MCHXs are quite small, requiring at least 500 units to meet the heat transfer surface area and PCM volume requirements. This becomes a problem because the available inlet tubes are perpendicular to the serpentine tube (Figure 24(b)), requiring excessive labor to cut, braze, and assemble the thermal battery for the 500+ serpentine MCHXs. Given these challenges, it was suggested that all-aluminum tube-fin coils be used. Rheem provided two tube-fin HXs, with different fin densities, 13-FPI and 16-FPI. To meet the required capacity of 17 kW (cooling mode) for 2 hours, the number of required HXs was calculated. The results show that the 13-FPI tube-fin HX is more convenient, as only 32 are required, whereas 112 are needed for the 16-FPI HX to accommodate the required PCM volume. Therefore, it was decided that the HX array would be assembled in two parallel rows of 16 HXs each, with a single inlet and a single outlet manifold for each row. To reduce manufacturing costs, two commercially-available bins were procured to serve as TES tanks, which will contain the phase change material (PCM) and HX array (Figure 25). The complete TES system comprises two bins, each composed of 16 HXs and one-half the PCM volume. All HXs and bins are connected in parallel. Page 30 of 127 DE-EE0009681 University of Maryland, College Park Figure 25: Procured TES Containers To connect the PCM-HXs in parallel, two manifolds were designed and manufactured. The manifolds for each TES are depicted in green (Figure 26). The four manifolds are identical except for the fittings at the end. The bins will be connected in parallel, with the inlet on the top right and the outlet on the bottom left. All other ends are fitted with a barbed hose connection to complete the circuitry. Each manifold has 16 x 3” long stubs (3/8” OD) that connect to the HX ports via Swagelok fittings. Note that the manifolds are modular, and thus any battery circuitry could be achieved by simply reorienting the manifold circuit (Figure 27). Figure 26: Two sets of the TES with Manifolds The two TES tanks were insulated to reduce heat loss during testing. The coated HXs were placed inside the tanks and supported by plastic studs. The copper manifolds were aligned with the HXs; however, misalignment between the HX ports and manifold stubs caused extreme bending stresses that broke the manifolds. Thus, nylon manifolds with threaded connections were sourced to connect the HXs (Figure 28).
